title: How should policing in Wales change?
label: 18 November 2026 · Wales’s police chiefs on reform
summary: The four Welsh chief constables described how they organise local policing, respond to misconduct and investigate violence against women. They supported some proposals to share technology and specialist work more widely, but questioned whether merging forces would improve local services. North Wales’s chief constable disputed the idea that one force for Wales was the best option. All four said the costs and practical effects of reform need much closer examination.

glossary.definition: The part of council tax raised locally to pay for policing.
A government document setting out proposed policies before detailed legislation.
Elected officials who oversee police forces, set priorities and help decide their budgets.
Transferred from the UK Government’s responsibility to the Welsh Government’s.

chapters.title: Different ways to police locally
chapters.takeaway: Gwent has reorganised around specialist teams, while the other forces say locally led areas suit their communities.

turns.speaker: Gerald Jones
turns.text: How does each force organise local policing? Mark, what evidence shows that Gwent’s switch away from locally based units improved its performance?

evidence.quote: Will you talk about what policing model each of the forces operates under, and whether there are any operational trade-offs associated with each model?
Will you talk a little bit about that, and what evidence there is for that improvement?

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: There’s no model that suits every force. In Gwent, separate local areas had been working rather like different forces, and officers were expected to handle everything from the first response through to court. I reorganised the force into teams for immediate policing, investigations and neighbourhood work, so people could specialise.

evidence.quote: there is no one-size-fits-all model that all police forces and police chief constables would agree was the best deliverable for their local community.

it felt very much like there were different forces operating in different ways. It also did not have specialised functions, so omni-competence was expected of our officers from the very start, when they went on patrol and dealt with an incident, right through to submitting files to courts and attending courts themselves.
I have three distinct pillars: an operational pillar, a crime pillar and a bespoke neighbourhood pillar.

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: Two and a half years ago, we met our 15-minute emergency response target and 60-minute priority response target about 45% and 48% of the time. Since the change, both have consistently been above 80%. Call-answering has also improved, and a recent survey found that 70% of respondents had confidence in Gwent Police. Those results and the feedback I get tell me the model fits Gwent.

evidence.quote: About two and a half years ago we were towards the bottom end of the 43 forces across England and Wales on metrics for responding to 999 and 101 calls. We are now consistently, over the last 12 months, in the top five forces
Two and a half years ago we were hitting metrics of about 45% and 48% success in those two arenas. Since changing to a functional model, we consistently deliver on those metrics over 80% of the time.
70% of those surveyed from our public said they have confidence in Gwent police.
on the metrics I see and the feedback I have, that is a model that fits Gwent.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: South Wales is divided into three large policing areas, with smaller local areas and inspectors beneath them. That gives local partners someone they know while allowing senior teams to oversee services across a wider area. We think it’s the right balance for us.

evidence.quote: Basically, we have those three core units. The local level sitting below them are local policing areas and local policing inspectors.
For us, the basic command unit model works because it strikes the right balance between local oversight and accountability, and local delivery.
the local policing area inspectors ought to be the immediate contact for local policing priorities and local partners, and then they feed up to a senior management team that sits above them.

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: North Wales also has three large areas, with smaller districts beneath them. We set staffing according to population and crime levels, but keep local leaders visible and connected to councils. That arrangement works for the different communities across north Wales.

evidence.quote: In North Wales, we have three basic command units: Eastern, which has the current local authorities of Wrexham and Flintshire in it, with four policing districts sitting under that; Central, which has Conwy and Denbighshire, with three areas underneath it; and the Western side is Gwynedd and Anglesey, with three areas in there.
we have very much tried to make sure that our resourcing and staffing levels across areas reflect the population and the crime levels that we see in those areas.
we find that the main strengths lie in maintaining visible local leadership, strong community relationships, effective partnership working, and responsiveness to our communities.

turns.speaker: Ifan Charles
turns.text: Dyfed-Powys has four areas matching its four councils. Each area’s senior officer is responsible for local performance and relationships with councils and health services. That gives people a clear answer to who is accountable.

evidence.quote: we have four basic command units, which reflect the local authority areas: Ceredigion, Carmarthenshire, Pembrokeshire and Powys.

The leader of an area is a superintendent. As Amanda mentioned, the expectation on that leader is that they are accountable for the performance in the area, and for building strong relationships with key stakeholders, as well as the local authority and health board chief execs
I think that provides some real clarity, ownership and local accountability

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Has Gwent’s reorganisation also saved money? And if its results have improved so much, why haven’t the other Welsh forces adopted its model?

evidence.quote: Have you managed to make more operational and financial efficiencies as a result of that change?
How come Mark is an outlier? The stats that he has just shared are quite remarkable in terms of the transformation.

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: It’s too early to claim significant savings from the reorganisation: we haven’t changed our staffing numbers because of it. Gwent’s finances also benefit from being able to raise more through the local council tax charge for policing, unlike forces in England, where that charge is capped.

evidence.quote: It is not significant, but I think what will happen over time is that we will potentially undertake more of a review of some of those posts within our response model, to tailor it accordingly. It is too early at the moment. We have not changed our establishment as a result of changing the operating model.
because of the flexibility allowed within Wales not to have the precept cap that England has, we have found ourselves in a position to up our precept accordingly

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: All four Welsh forces received the top grade in the latest police inspection, and we face different demands. I’ve brought a Gwent approach to preparing domestic abuse cases into North Wales, but that doesn’t mean Gwent’s entire structure would suit our more rural area.

evidence.quote: If you look at the latest HMIC assessment of performance, we are all graded in the top category. We all police different areas.
One of the things that we did when I was in Gwent was the file-based domestic abuse team. That was something that worked really well and I have taken that with me to North Wales
My force in particular is more rural than Gwent. It is right that I try to deliver the best policing model for the communities that we serve across north Wales.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: Response times matter, but they aren’t the only test. We also need to look at investigation results and how forces handle sexual violence. Across those measures, we think our current South Wales structure works best.

evidence.quote: It is not just our ability to respond, which is a really important one; it is our outcome rate, it is how we respond to sexual violence.
as it stands, we think that that model, for us, delivers the best performance across a range of indicators.

chapters.title: Trust starts inside the force
chapters.takeaway: The chiefs described checks, dismissals and efforts to make staff report misconduct, while acknowledging that the work is unfinished.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You’ve all talked about public trust. How do you check that you’re finding and dealing with misconduct by your own staff?

evidence.quote: How do you evaluate your force’s performance in clamping down on staff misconduct?
How are you evaluating your force’s performance? How are you managing staff?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: In South Wales, all staff vetting is up to date, and we have a team that investigates misconduct and corruption. Staff can pass on information confidentially. Since I became chief in 2020, 126 people have been dismissed. I also think there are still people working for me who’ve behaved improperly, including racists and misogynists; we have to find and remove them.

evidence.quote: We are 100% compliant, with all our vetting up to date.
having a well-resourced and equipped professional standards department, which includes an anti-corruption capability.
We have a confidential Crimestoppers internal intelligence line that people can use.
I have been the chief since 2020, and 126 people have been dismissed under my watch.

Do I think I have people who have misconducted themselves working for me? Yes. Do I think I have racists and misogynists working for me? Yes. Do I think my work is to find them and excommunicate them from policing? Absolutely yes.

turns.speaker: Ifan Charles
turns.text: In Dyfed-Powys, some staff are being investigated for serious misconduct, including misogynistic behaviour. We’ve also asked staff to commit to calling out bad behaviour. I discuss that expectation with new officers and supervisors, and it’s part of deciding who gets promoted. It can’t just be words on a poster.

evidence.quote: I also have people being investigated for gross misconduct, and some who are also suspended. Some of those are for misogynistic behaviours, so we are taking robust action against them.
we call out bad behaviour, and we always try to be better tomorrow.
That cannot be a poster on the wall with just words on it
I speak at every PC tutor course, every PCSO tutor course and every-first line and second-line leader course.
It is also the presentation topic for all our promotion processes

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: I brought in outside help to assess North Wales Police’s culture, and staff can raise concerns directly with me. We’ve removed officers through misconduct procedures and during their initial probation period. We also use vetting and information from the public to identify people who don’t meet the standards.

evidence.quote: I did a huge amount of work around the culture of our organisation, which included working with an outside organisation to be able to evaluate it fully.
I host an ongoing “Ask the Chief”, where I am available to anybody within the force to ring in, call in or do a Teams meeting and ask any question.

they have been through a misconduct process. I have also had a number of officers where I have utilised regulation 13 to dispense with their services, because they are not likely to become a well-conducted officer during their probationary period.
including making full use of the vetting regime we have in place.
in terms of anti-corruption, information from the public, and how we deal with people who do not live up to the standards.

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: Gwent had senior leaders whose behaviour didn’t belong in policing; they were removed and faced consequences. Our outstanding misconduct cases have fallen from 47 in August to 37, and suspensions from 19 to 14. In a staff survey, more than 90% gave positive answers to questions about reporting misconduct and whether it would be taken seriously. That encourages me, but the work isn’t finished.

evidence.quote: There were some very high-profile senior leaders within Gwent policing who did not represent the values of modern-day policing, and they were quite rightly removed from the organisation and faced consequences.
if you go back to August, we had 47 misconduct cases; we now have 37 outstanding. We had 19 people suspended, and we now have 14 suspended.
All those metrics were well in excess of 90%; two of the questions were in excess of 95%.
that does not at all mean that we are a finished product.

chapters.title: Protecting victims under pressure
chapters.takeaway: Forces are changing how they support victims and pursue offenders, but growing demand and rural distances complicate the work.

turns.speaker: Ann Davies
turns.text: What progress are you making on violence against women and girls, and how do you measure it?

evidence.quote: I am going to move on to violence against women and girls.
What progress has your force made towards that goal? How are you measuring that progress?
Does that mean knife crime and VAWG?
Both, yes.

turns.speaker: Ifan Charles
turns.text: In Dyfed-Powys, domestic abuse victims can sometimes speak to a specialist remotely at a safer time and place. An independent adviser is also working in our call centre as part of a trial. We’re working with other organisations to manage people who may pose a continuing risk, including some who haven’t been convicted. Our rates of charging suspects in domestic abuse and sexual offence cases have improved over the last two or three years.

evidence.quote: We have a domestic abuse virtual response unit, for example, which means we can communicate at a time and place that is more suitable for a victim of domestic abuse when reporting.
we have an independent domestic abuse adviser now based in our control rooms. That is a pilot we are running at Dyfed-Powys.
working with other agencies to manage the risk posed by offenders within the community. Those may be unconvicted offenders who may have had a number of domestic abuse incidents reported against them.
In terms of our charge rates for those things, which is when people are charged and go to court, we have seen an improvement over the last two or three years

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: North Wales has reviewed its specialist teams. We’ve also set up a team to get domestic abuse case paperwork right the first time, so fewer victims drop out before a case can proceed; charging outcomes have improved significantly. We work with sexual assault advisers and have a specialist team for stalking and harassment, which is a growing concern.

evidence.quote: We have just done a quite extensive review of our public protection teams to make sure we can respond effectively.

I introduced a domestic abuse file unit to make sure we get the paperwork side of things right first time to reduce victim attrition. Our charge outcome rate has increased in relation to this area significantly.

We have a sexual assault referral centre that we use, and it is linked to independent sexual violence advisers. We have a dedicated multi-agency team to look at stalking and harassment. That is a growing area of real public concern

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: Gwent has a programme for partners of police employees who experience domestic abuse. Some had feared the force wouldn’t investigate one of its own. Dedicated staff now support them from reporting through to the investigation’s conclusion. More people are reporting, including abuse from the past. But nationally, successful outcomes for rape and serious sexual offences still aren’t where they should be.

evidence.quote: Taboo is for partners of serving police officers or members of staff who may be subjected to domestic violence, enabling them to report effectively what they are being subjected to.
some victims had found a lack of confidence in reporting, feeling that they were reporting to an agency that might not want to root out one of its own.
bespoke officers working within our professional standards departments, who assist a person in such a circumstance from reporting right through to the end result of that investigation
we are seeing an increase in reporting. Those are sometimes historical matters
positive outcome detection rates for rape and serious sexual offences are not where they should be.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: We’re getting better results from specialist sexual offence teams, and remote contact can work better when it suits the victim and the perpetrator isn’t there. But reported rape and serious sexual offences have risen sharply over the past decade, and many offences may still go unreported. Victims need time and support, especially when court cases are delayed. With our current resources, we can’t give everyone the service they deserve.

evidence.quote: That is not when the perpetrator is there; it is on the victim’s terms where we can contact them remotely, and all the data indicates that it gives better outcomes and better confidence levels. We have rape and serious sexual offences teams delivering much better outcomes than they have ever delivered before.
some studies suggest three in four crimes of violence against women go unreported. In the last 10 years, we have seen a 461% increase in rape and serious sexual offences.
We cannot give the service that we need with the resources we have available to us. People need us to spend more time with them.
building their confidence in a criminal justice system that has loads of delays.

turns.speaker: Ann Davies
turns.text: Ifan, across such a large rural area, where would you put a dedicated team to investigate rape?

evidence.quote: Where would you see that dedicated space being, bearing in mind that you cover an area from Newtown down to Llanelli and over to Pembroke?

turns.speaker: Ifan Charles
turns.text: We’re working towards a dedicated team by the end of 2027. It couldn’t all sit in one place: trained specialists would need to be based around Dyfed-Powys, probably in the stations where staff are now.

evidence.quote: Our plan is to work towards having a dedicated rape investigation team by the end of 2027
you have to have staff based in those local areas, so you would not be able to centralise that team.

That would then be allocated to a rape specialist with all the right training and accreditations to be able to deal compassionately with the victim. They would have to be based across the Dyfed-Powys area, probably at the stations where we have them now.

chapters.title: Reform without losing local service
chapters.takeaway: The chiefs see benefits in shared national capabilities but want evidence that changing force boundaries would help rather than weaken local policing.

turns.speaker: David Chadwick
turns.text: The Government’s White Paper sets out problems with policing and proposes changes. Do you agree with its diagnosis, and will its proposals solve those problems?

evidence.quote: Do you agree with the issues that the White Paper diagnoses? How confident are you that the proposed reforms will solve those issues?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: Broadly, yes on the problems. A stronger national service could help forces buy and use technology together. Mergers might also save money, but I haven’t seen all the reviews or legislation. Any change must be funded, given a realistic timetable and judged by whether it improves the service people receive locally.

evidence.quote: I agree, broadly speaking, with the issues that the White Paper raises. Do I know whether the proposals will address the problems? Well, what I have not seen yet is the outcome of a number of reviews, nor the legislation in its entirety.
a stronger national centre of policing? I do, because I think it will help us to develop, procure and apply the best technology

Do I think that a restructure of forces could deliver efficiencies? Yes; however, we were clear in our submission that it has to be properly funded, the timescale ahead needs to be realistic and the objective must be to improve local policing services.

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: A national service makes sense for online crime that crosses force boundaries, and forces could buy some equipment more cheaply together. But that’s a separate question from merging local forces. I haven’t seen evidence that a merger would benefit Gwent or a convincing account of how it would be paid for. If it forced us back into separate council-based areas, I think performance could suffer.

evidence.quote: The building of a national police service makes a lot of sense as we move into a future that is looking at far more cyber and borderless crime
we could get better procurement buying certain things en masse, from the perspective of technology and some other assets.
a national police service, a White Paper reform and a structural change are all very different subjects.

I have not seen an evidenced business case to support a structural change that would give me satisfaction about the benefits we would have in Gwent, geographically. I have certainly not seen any financial assurance that this could be deliverable.
for Gwent that could potentially mean going to five local authorities, which would be a backward step for me in performance and deliverables.

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: I support sharing some national services, but I’m genuinely worried about forced mergers. North Wales works closely with forces in north-west England because crime often comes into our area from the east. I need to know how those relationships and rural services would be protected, and whether money raised locally would be taken to fund a national service.

evidence.quote: I also collaborate extensively with the north-west region: Merseyside, Cheshire, Cumbria, Lancashire and Greater Manchester.
the criminality that comes into north Wales travels from the east to the west, not from the south to the north.
I am genuinely concerned about the prospect of forced mergers because of that difference that we see in north Wales.
Anything that is centralised tends to reduce service in our rural communities
I agree with the concept of a national police service that sits across the top of policing and allows us to have better buying power.
I still have question marks about how that is top sliced from forces’ budgets and where that comes from in our local communities.

turns.speaker: Ifan Charles
turns.text: There are useful ideas in the White Paper, including better training for neighbourhood policing and a national service. But we haven’t been given evidence for changing force boundaries. We’d also need to understand the cost of change and what happens to different staff pay and council tax levels.

evidence.quote: There are other bits in the White Paper that are really positive, such as making sure that neighbourhood policing and the training around it is professionalised, “right care, right person”, increasing the number of volunteers, leadership, workforce, and the national police service.
we have not really been given an evidenced-based reason for why force structures need to change.
the equalisation of pay of police staff and funding of the change. Council tax equalisation would also need to be considered.

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: National priorities don’t always match what people raise locally. In Gwent, people want visible officers and repeatedly complain about off-road bikes. A reform must leave us able to respond to those concerns as well as national ones.

evidence.quote: they want to see visible people on their streets—people who care about their neighbourhoods. For me, that has to be strongly maintained.
the top five concerns that our communities across Gwent have are not mirroring the national objectives.

We have to walk that tightrope of meeting national objectives, which we all agree are really important, while also meeting local community needs. You do not see off-road biking as a top concern among the national objectives, but in Gwent, every one of our community councils will have that as a top priority.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: Reform won’t fix everything. Complex investigations and vulnerable victims need more officer time. We think Welsh policing gets about £100 million less in government grant than it should, and local taxpayers have had to make up part of the gap through the precept. Whatever structure we end up with, Wales needs enough funding.

evidence.quote: There are the increases in complexity and vulnerability and the time we should be spending with people but are not able to, and I am not sure that reform is going to fix that in its entirety.
Turning to Wales, we think that we are £100 million light on the allocation of grant to policing in Wales.
We have had go to the police and crime commissioner, and by extension the local taxpayer, to ask for more precept year on year
we need to make sure that policing in Wales is sufficiently funded

turns.speaker: Simon Hoare
turns.text: If forces are merged, is one police force for all Wales the likely answer? And how would a single force make sure rural areas get a fair service when crime figures may direct resources towards cities?

evidence.quote: if the force mergers go ahead, it is more than likely that Wales would see one constabulary, rather like Northern Ireland and Scotland?
how will rural Wales feel that it gets a decent enough slice of the resources cake when the data will point to the urban areas having the higher rates of crime

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: The Home Office asked us to compare options with fewer than four Welsh forces; keeping all four wasn’t an option in that exercise. After examining one, two and three-force models, our work concluded that one force was the best of those reduced-force options.

evidence.quote: we were given a task by the Home Office as a group of chief constables to design what the best model for Wales would be, with the underlying prerogative that it would be a reduced number of police forces. An as-is model was not an option for us
we concluded that a one-force Wales was the best of a reduced police force model

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: I don’t agree that one force is best for Wales. We were asked, ‘If not four, what?’ rather than what would work best. I don’t see a problem with the current arrangement. If it must change, two forces is an option I’d consider. My concern is that a single force could leave remote north Wales communities isolated, despite their stronger road links to north-west England.

evidence.quote: I do not agree that it is the best option for Wales, but we have been given the opportunity to put into an independent review, and the question we were asked was not: “What do you think is best for Wales?” It was: “If it is not four, what would it be?”
I do not see an issue with the current way we are delivering the policing

Your second question about delivering to rural communities becomes significantly at risk by going to one force for Wales. I am concerned about the vulnerability and isolation that we would see in the farthest part of north Wales, which is disconnected from the point of view of road infrastructure and the ability to travel and is more connected to the north-west of England.
From my perspective, that would be one of the options that I would have.

turns.speaker: Steve Witherden
turns.text: You wrote to the head of the National Police Chiefs’ Council about senior police leaders’ interventions on restructuring. What concerned you?

evidence.quote: You recently wrote to the head of the National Police Chiefs’ Council to outline your concerns and frustrations with the interventions made by senior police leaders regarding force restructuring, as we have just been discussing. Could you expand on those concerns for us, please?

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: I wanted it understood that not every force serves a big city. Coastal, rural and urban communities have different problems. I’m responsible for north Wales, so I needed its experience to be represented when police leaders discussed the options.

evidence.quote: we have to recognise that communities do not exist in that way and that policing is there to deliver good policing to local communities, whether they are coastal, rural or urban.
those communities have very different problems, which they look to us in policing to resolve.
I am policing the citizens of north Wales. I am employed to do that, and it is right that I put my representations forward on their behalf
I wanted to ensure that the NPCC, in having that discussion, had that broad understanding of what we are all contending with, which is different.

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: Scotland’s merger offers a warning: from what I’ve heard, it was rushed and lost focus on local policing. Others there judge the eventual service more positively. If Wales changes, we need enough time and money, and a clear promise about the service people can expect wherever they live.

evidence.quote: From those I have spoken to in Scotland, the experience of the Scottish Institute for Policing Research is quite a good point of reference. It would say that it took its eye off local policing; it was focused and had six months to make a decision and deliver mergers.

Sir Ian Livingstone, who left that role in 2023, wrote a long article for one of the media outlets where he gave his analysis of the last 10 years. He would say policing in Scotland is better as a result of the mergers
if you are going to do a change, you must invest in it, focus on local first, and do it in a realistic timeframe.
It must be the most important thing to provide a service to people wherever they are and wherever they live

chapters.title: Sharing services and deciding who oversees them
chapters.takeaway: The chiefs described savings from cooperation but said wider changes to oversight or Welsh Government responsibility depend on practical safeguards.

turns.speaker: Ben Lake
turns.text: Could the forces save more by working together rather than merging? What examples do you already have?

evidence.quote: are we missing something a bit obvious—that there may well be further opportunities for collaboration to realise some financial savings and to address the supposed inefficiencies? If so, do you have anything to add, and any examples to which you could refer the Committee

turns.speaker: Ifan Charles
turns.text: Forces already share specialist services, including a firearms unit. A particularly useful opportunity is buying forensic services together: previously, different groups of forces had separate arrangements, which was inefficient and let suppliers play us off against one another. We’ve now brought those purchasing arrangements together. The test must be whether the public and victims benefit.

evidence.quote: We have a joint firearms unit; we do that jointly, and all our staff utilise the different parts of the estate that we have.
It was a 15-force collaboration. We needed to merge that with the direct purchasing system under BlueLight Commercial.

That was inefficient in the way we were dealing with the private sector, but also it was able to play us off against one another. So we worked collectively—together—and we are now merged on to one deep direct purchasing system under BlueLight Commercial.
there have to be benefits for victims and the public in what we are trying to achieve. That is the test for all of it.

turns.speaker: Amanda Blakeman
turns.text: North Wales shares systems and purchasing with other forces and has saved more than £40 million over several years. We can do more, including with forces across the English border. But buying everything nationally could move jobs and skills away from Welsh communities.

evidence.quote: we already do a lot of collaboration. I am talking about purchasing vehicles, frameworks that we are on in terms of collaborations nationally, and IT collaborations that we have. In North Wales alone, we have saved more than £40 million over a number of years.
For North Wales, there will be more to do in the north-west of England—as much as there is to do in Wales.
As soon as we procure once nationally, we tend to find that we lose services from our local area. It is important that we retain that talent within our forces and local communities.

turns.speaker: Mark Hobrough
turns.text: My preferred approach is a national service for things best done together, alongside more shared specialist teams. Gwent has recently expanded its forensic partnership and started bringing its computer systems together with South Wales Police. But I’d keep neighbourhood officers, emergency response, local investigators and misconduct teams within local forces.

evidence.quote: What you have described would be my preferred model—an overarching, national police service with some of the abilities that we discussed earlier, including regional capability through collaborative agreements.

we have gone from a joint scientific investigation unit, which Gwent and South Wales shared, to a forensic alliance that includes Dyfed-Powys. Also recently, we have gone from a Gwent IT system, shared with local authority partners, to an IT convergence with South Wales within Gwent
There are certain things that I think should have—for want of a better phrase—red lines around them, such as neighbourhood policing, response policing, CID and our own PSDs.

turns.speaker: Llinos Medi
turns.text: The Government plans to replace police and crime commissioners. What should take their place, and what do you think of the Welsh commissioners’ proposal?

evidence.quote: We know that the UK Government are replacing the crime commissioners

In your opinion, what should replace them? Secondly, the Welsh PCCs have outlined their own ideas about this, and they have some trade-offs. What risks and opportunities are associated with their proposals for police accountability in Wales?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: The commissioners consulted us closely about their proposal. We thought their preferred option offered the best balance between public oversight and allowing chiefs to make operational decisions. But chiefs shouldn’t decide who oversees them.

evidence.quote: On the model submission they made, they consulted heavily with us. They sought our views on the implications for operational independence and for conducting the role of chief heavily.
it would be wrong in every way for us to decide our own governance.

the so-called model D—was the model that we agreed offered the best balance between the business of policing being allowed to continue while respecting operational independence, and the right level of democratic accountability and oversight

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Should responsibility for policing be devolved to the Welsh Government?

evidence.quote: Do we think that policing should be devolved to the Welsh Government?

turns.speaker: Jeremy Vaughan
turns.text: That’s a political decision, not one for us. It might bring police priorities closer to those of other Welsh public services, but I’d need to see the funding, oversight, arrangements for working across borders and continued national support before saying it would work. I haven’t seen a detailed proposal.

evidence.quote: First, it is a political decision, isn’t it? That one is definitely out of our hands, but what we can do is describe its operational implications.

We would want to be satisfied that the funding was right, that the governance was right and that the operational interfaces we all have in our different ways were right across the board, and we would still need support from a national service.
I think we could see better alignment of priorities in Wales between policing and other partners
I have not seen the proposal, so I have not seen all those things laid out.
